slides.title: Most newborn jaundice is normal.
slides.title2: Some of it ==damages the brain==. Know which.
slides.sub: The rules that decide, plus the **one hour-of-life** that is never normal.

slides.title: Physiological jaundice
rows: Unconjugated: high RBC turnover, immature liver
Feed often. Plot TSB on the **hour-specific chart**

slides.title: Pathological jaundice
slides.tagline: any one of these. go looking for a cause.
rows: Above the phototherapy line for age in hours
Pale stools, dark urine, sick or lethargic baby

slides.title: Breastfeeding vs breast milk
rows: **Week 1**. Too little milk: poor intake, weight loss, fewer wet nappies
Feed **8–12 times a day**, check latch
Starts **after week 1**, peaks weeks 2–3, baby thriving
**Continue breastfeeding**. Rule out other causes first

slides.text: ==Never physiological.== Jaundice seen in the **first 24 hours** needs a serum bilirubin now, not tomorrow.
slides.note: Commonest cause: haemolysis (Rh or ABO incompatibility).
slides.note_hand: check mother's & baby's blood group + DCT

caption:
Most newborn jaundice is normal. Some of it damages the brain. Here is how to tell them apart 👶💛

✅ Physiological: appears after 24 h, peaks day 3–5 (term), gone by ~1 week (term) / 2 weeks (preterm), baby well
🚩 Pathological, any one: visible in the first 24 h · rise > 0.2 mg/dL/h · above the phototherapy line · conjugated > 1 mg/dL · > 2 wk term / > 3 wk preterm · pale stools, dark urine
🤱 Breastfeeding jaundice (week 1, low intake → feed 8–12×/day) vs breast milk jaundice (after week 1, peaks weeks 2–3 → continue breastfeeding)

The rule: jaundice in the first 24 hours is never normal. Check blood groups + DCT and send a serum bilirubin now.

Day 1 yellow: never normal. Fast rise: think haemolysis. Week 3 yellow: check the stool.

💾 Save for your next postnatal round
📩 Send to the intern on nights
💬 What cause do you see most in your NICU?

For medical education. Verify with current guidelines and your unit protocol.
